desc: Handling of animals.
narrative:
The post and rail barrier fence surrounding the reindeer enclosure has several posts and rails that are broken, missing, or
lying on the ground. Exhibit is not currently open to the public this time of year. Public exhibition of animals must be
handled so that there is minimal risk of harm to the animal and to the public, with sufficient distance and/or barriers
between the animal and the public so as to protect the safety of the animal and pubic. The barrier fence surrounding the
reindeer must be repaired or replaced to protect the health of the animal and public. Correct by October 15, 2021.

desc: RECORDS: DEALERS AND EXHIBITORS.
narrative:
Currently the list of Animals on Hand has not been updated and is not available during this inspection. The
information of the animals born and sold are being kept, however there needs to be some clarification of the
information to make the traceability more accurate.
Complete and accurate records are necessary for proper management and traceability of the regulated animals on
Hand and those sold.
The licensee must keep updated and accurate records of all Animals on Hand, and those that are sold with the
appropriate information required according to sections 2.75 of the AWA regulations and standards.
To be corrected by: August 7, 2015

desc: WATERING.
narrative:
The water tank for the wallaby area has a moderate to thick buildup of dark green algae along the sides and bottom
of the tank.
A buildup of algae in the water tank can be a source of possible disease or health hazards if not cleaned and
sanitized properly.
The licensee must clean the water tank as frequently as necessary to prevent the buildup of algae and keep the
tank and drinking water clean and sanitary.
To be corrected by: June 29, 2015

desc: SANITATION.
narrative:
The goat platform has a hole in the boarded floor approximately 1ft x 2 ft that opens to the ground approximately 3
feet down that needs to be repaired. There are several nails along the edge of the platform and near the stairs that
need to be hammered in or removed that have worked their way up and are protruding 1-2 inches. There is a fence
gate lying on the ground in the camel feeding yard, and two pet carriers and some yard tools in the wallaby area
that need to be removed as they are un-necessary clutter in the animal yards.
The hole and nails on the goat platform could be a potential source of injury if an animal fell through the hole in the
floor or snagged on one of the protruding nails. The clutter in the camel and wallaby yards could cause injury if the
animals get caught up in the fence lying on the ground, or trip over the yard tools(pitchfork, shovel, old can, brush,
carriers etc).
The licensee needs to repair the goat platform and pick up and remove any clutter in the areas where the regulated
animals live.
To be corrected by: July 5, 2015
Inspection and Exit interview conducted with facility representative.

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
narrative:
The August 2022 and February 2023 semi-annual reports to the Institutional Official (IO) were not signed by a majority of
the IACUC members. Semiannual reports to the Institutional Official inform the IO of the current status of the animal
program and facilities. The semiannual reports must be reviewed and signed by a majority of the IACUC members, and
must include any minority views. This demonstrates consensus amongst the IACUC members, allows the opportunity for
communication of any minority views, and helps to ensure animal health and well-being.
Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC)
narrative:
The amendment pertaining to the change of the principal investigator for protocol #99-01 was approved using email
replies from the IACUC members. Appropriate IACUC review is necessary to safeguard the use of all animals in studies
and ensures the protocols are in compliance with the Animal Welfare Act and Regulations. The IACUC shall review
proposed activities involving the care and use of animals and any member can call for a full Committee review. If not, the
chairman can designate a member to review and have the authority to approve, modify or request full Committee review
of any of those activities. No member may participate in IACUC review or approval of an activity in which that member is
personally involved in the activity or has a conflict in interest.
Correct by August 31, 2023.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the authorized person.
Additional Inspectors:
SUSANNE BRUNKHORST, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
narrative:
Dogs used on protocol #02-22 underwent a terminal anesthesia procedure and increased volume blood draw that were
not defined in the IACUC approved protocol. The addition of the procedures were approved by the attending veterinarian
rather than the IACUC. The facility does not have an IACUC approved policy in place for the attending veterinarian to
approve changes to a protocol on behalf of the IACUC. The IACUC shall review and approve, require modifications to
secure approval or withhold approval of proposed significant changes regarding the care and use of animals in ongoing
activities. Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC)
narrative:
Review of IACUC minutes disclosed that protocol #02-22 was reviewed and approved solely by email correspondence
from the IACUC. Appropriate IACUC review is necessary to safeguard the use of all animals on study. The IACUC shall
review proposed activities involving the care and use of animals and any member can call for a full Committee review. If
not, the chairman can designate a member to review and have the authority to approve, modify or request full Committee
review of any of those activities. No member may participate in IACUC review or approval of an activity in which that
member is personally involved in the activity.
Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
narrative:
Protocol #02-22 did not contain a rationale for the number of animals to be used. The study stated they would use sixteen
dogs total, dividing into subsets. This approach would ‘balance achieving statistical significance while minimizing the
number of dogs used’. No details such as statistical tests used or statisticians consulted were included to support the
statement. An animal use proposal must include a rationale for the appropriateness of the numbers of animals to be used
so that the IACUC can conduct a thorough review of the components of the activities related to the care and use of
animals and determine that the proposed activities are in accordance with the Animal Welfare Act. The proposal to
conduct an activity involving animals must contain a rationale for the numbers of animals to be used.
Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Recordkeeping requirements.
narrative:
The facility did not record the disposition information for sixteen dogs. Failure to maintain completed animal records
hinders accurate tracking, identification, and tracing of animals upon their removal from the current facility. Every research
facility shall keep and maintain records for live dogs which fully and correctly disclose the required information for the
transporting, selling, or otherwise disposing of any live dog.
Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Exercise for dogs.
narrative:
The registrant did not develop and document a written exercise plan for sixteen dogs used on study #02-22. Exercise is
important for the well-being of the dogs. Research facilities must develop, document, and follow an appropriate plan to
provide dogs with the opportunity for exercise. In addition, the plan must be approved by the attending veterinarian and
available during APHIS inspections for review.
Correct by August 31, 2023.

desc: Veterinary care for dogs.
narrative:
The facility does not have a documented program of veterinary care. The facility completed a study, housing and using
dogs in February 2023. The absence of a program of veterinary care disallows assurance that the preventive care and
treatment is aligned with the veterinarian's authority and guidance. A written Program of Veterinary Care (PVC) for dogs
must be established and maintained so that the facility has a current plan that provides for adequate preventative care
and treatments as deemed necessary. The plan must include all required components as listed in the Animal Welfare Act
and Animal Welfare Regulations, Part 3, Subpart A, Section 3.13.
Correct by August 31, 2023.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with authorized person.
Additional Inspectors:
SUSANNE BRUNKHORST, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n

desc: INSTITUTIONAL ANIMAL CARE AND USE COMMITTEE (IACUC).
narrative:

stating if they are critical or minor, stating if there are any minority reports, and signed by a majority of the IACUC
members. To be corrected with future reports.
Exit briefing conducted with facility representative.

desc: Housing facilities, general.
narrative:
An opened bag of Cheerios and dried cranberries used for feeding enrichment were stored on a shelf in the enrichment
area and countertop in the processing room, respectively. Neither food item had been placed in a container with a fitted lid
after opening. Failure to appropriately store supplied food items can compromise the nutritive value of the food items
provided to the animals, as well as enable easier access by bugs and pests to infiltrate the bags of food. All open supplies
of food and bedding must be kept in leakproof containers with tightly fitted lids. Only food and bedding that is currently
being used may be kept in the animal areas. Supplies of food and bedding must be stored off the floor and away from the
walls, to allow cleaning underneath and around the supplies.
Correct by September 5, 2024.

desc: Sheltered housing facilities.
narrative:
Multiple areas along the perimeter fence no longer stand at six feet tall at the facility. Upon inspection, one area measured
as low as 59.5 inches at the gate between the front building and left side of the perimeter fence. Additionally, a 7.5 inch
gap was observed between the ground and bottom of the fence near the Field Cage 10 building.
Having a perimeter fence in place protects the animals in the facility by restricting animals and unauthorized persons from
going through it or under it, permitting contact with the animals in the facility. Additionally, it serves as a secondary
containment system for the animals in the facility.
The perimeter fence must be of sufficient distance from the outside of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact
between animals inside the enclosure and animals or persons outside the perimeter fence. Non-dangerous animals
housed in outdoor facilities require a 6-foot-tall perimeter fence around their enclosure and must be at least 3-feet away
from any enclosures or buildings, unless an approved variance has been issued in writing by the Administrator.
Correct by September 5, 2024.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the authorized person.
n

desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
narrative:
Upon inspection, one vial of “Humulin N” insulin was still being utilized beyond the recommended packaging timeframe
and confirmed by the facility representative present that the medication was still being given to animals on-hand. The
instructions on the box denote that any unused portion remaining 31 days after first opening should be discarded. The
open vial identified was opened on August 6, 2023, and still being administered to two diabetic primates.
Medications may lose their strength and may no longer be effective as indicated for their use when used outside of the
designated time table identified by the manufacturer. Additionally, the effect of the medications may be unpredictable,
potentially leading to further illness when used beyond the intended time outlined on the label. The facility must ensure
the availability of appropriate facilities, personnel, equipment, and services to comply with the provisions of this
subchapter.
The facility corrected during the inspection.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with authorized person.

desc: ATTENDING VETERINARIAN AND ADEQUATE VETERINARY CARE (DEALERS AND EXHIBITORS).
narrative:
A 14 year old male cynomologus, number 1824, is not using his rear legs at all. He is exhibiting contracted stiff
legs, and moves around with his forelegs. No lesions were observable from cage side. There are no notations in his
medical record about this condition as to when did it start, is it getting worse, or have any treatments been tried.
The new Attending Veterinarian needs to examine this animal and make suggestions for his care.
To be corrected by 3-24-17,

desc: FACILITIES, OUTDOOR.
narrative:
There are four groundhogs in individual cages housed outside. Since the last inspection, they were moved under a
roofed shelter. The property where the shelter is located only has a 4 - 5 foot livestock fence around it. A separate
6 foot perimeter fence located at least 3 feet away from the animal enclosures is required for all wild animals unless
a variance is obtained. To be corrected by 4-7-17.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted withTSS President and Facilities Manager.

desc: FACILITIES, GENERAL.
narrative:
The metal support bars under the outdoor wire cages for two banks of 27 rabbits are excessively rusting and
actually missing parts of the bars. These bars are no longer structurally sound nor can they be sanitized and need
to be replaced. To be corrected by 8-19-16.

desc: SPACE REQUIREMENTS.
narrative:
A new species was added since the last inspection. Groundhogs are now being housed here in metal bar cages.
One groundhog was in a different cage which was more like a tunnel, but only provided 13 inches of vertical height.
These are large full grown groundhogs and a normal postural adjustment is to stand up on rear legs. Enclosures
need to provide sufficient space to allow each animal to make normal postural and social adjustments with
adequate freedom of movement. During this inspection additional space was added to double the size of this
enclosure, thus correcting this deficiency.
Exit briefing conducted with facility representative.

desc: ATTENDING VETERINARIAN AND ADEQUATE VETERINARY CARE (DEALERS AND EXHIBITORS).
narrative:
Dutch belted rabbits are being bred at the facility and four does and their unweaned kits are in indoor cages today.
All of the 13 unweaned kits and 6 weaned rabbits (including 3 outside) have severely splayed rear legs. They can
not pull their rear legs under their body and hop normally. Instead they mostly pull themselves with their forelegs
and drag their rears. One of the outside rabbits has splayed foreleg and rear legs, and it was observed paddling
around the cage. The caretakers state they have tried various solid surfaces in the indoor slat metal floor cages,
but nothing helped.
The attending veterinarian was not aware of this condition as he has not been consulted about it. The female
rabbits are culls from a breeder and because this condition is believed to be partially congenital, this may be the
reason for the cull. Although no lesions were observed on the rabbits and they are able to move around to reach
food and water, treatments need to be attempted to decrease the severity of the splay legs. Besides treating the
legs, different habitats and surfaces could be tried to help the current splayed rabbits with mobility. These rabbits
are generally not kept for more than 3 - 6 months. To be corrected by 9-3-15.

desc: ENVIRONMENT ENHANCEMENT TO PROMOTE PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING.
narrative:
A singly housed male cynomologus macaque, number 9442 in room 2A has total fur loss in every area he can
reach. His entire front and lower back are bare. Alopecia can indicate potential psychological distress. This
primate is not receiving any special environmental enhancements over the routine ones being provided for all in the
room. This same male was cited in 2010, but there is no individual record to review showing if he has ever regrown
his fur from that time. In consult with the Attending Veterinarian, this primate's environment needs to be enhanced
or completely altered to attempt to stop the chronic fur loss. To be corrected by 9-14-15.
Exit briefing conducted with facility representative.

desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
narrative:
The IACUC conducted semi-annual program review and facility inspections in March 2023. A report of the IACUC's
